children: The 25 bps repo rate hike is likely to gradually raise funding costs for non-banking finance companies, putting greater focus on liquidity, pricing and disciplined credit growth

Non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) are likely to face a gradual increase in funding costs after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent and shifted its monetary policy stance to calibrated tightening.

The move marks the first repo rate increase since February 2023 and comes as the central bank responds to broadening inflation pressures while retaining a firm growth outlook. The RBI has raised its FY27 growth forecast to 7.1 per cent from 6.7 per cent.
For NBFCs, however, the immediate impact is less about a sharp repricing of their loan books and more about how funding markets respond to the change in policy direction.
Funding Costs To Rise Gradually

Rajiv Sabharwal, MD & CEO, Tata Capital, said the latest policy decision could gradually increase the cost of funds for NBFCs, although the extent would depend on liquidity conditions and market funding.
“NBFCs may see a gradual increase in funding costs depending on systemic liquidity and market conditions,” Sabharwal said.

This makes the funding mix particularly important for NBFCs. Companies that rely more heavily on market borrowings and other wholesale sources could see their cost of capital respond differently from those with more diversified funding structures.

The shift to calibrated tightening also makes the interest-rate environment less favourable for a sector that has benefited from relatively supportive financial conditions. NBFCs will now have to balance the need to maintain competitive lending rates with the need to protect spreads as their own funding costs move higher.
Sabharwal said the sector’s response should centre on maintaining funding resilience while continuing to expand credit prudently.
“Funding resilience, prudent risk management and disciplined credit growth will remain important,” he said.
Credit Demand Could Cushion The Impact

Higher funding costs do not necessarily imply a corresponding slowdown in credit demand. The domestic economy continues to show resilience, giving NBFCs room to maintain lending activity even as monetary conditions become tighter.

The RBI itself has raised its growth outlook, with first-quarter FY27 growth coming in stronger than expected. Bank credit growth has also remained robust, underlining continued demand for financing across the economy.

For NBFCs, this creates a trade-off. Stronger demand provides an opportunity to grow the loan book, but pursuing growth too aggressively when the cost of funds is rising could put pressure on profitability and risk-adjusted returns.
Rohit Arora, CEO & Co-founder, Biz2Credit and Biz2X, said the rate increase should not be viewed as a signal that businesses will suddenly stop borrowing.
“A 25 bps hike will not stop borrowing. Credit demand remains strong,” Arora said.
The more important consideration for lenders, he said, would be how they price individual borrowers as funding conditions change.
“Lenders will need to price risk borrower by borrower,” Arora said.
For NBFCs, that could mean greater differentiation between borrowers based on cash flows, business resilience and repayment capacity rather than relying on broad-based pricing assumptions.
Micro And Small Borrowers Remain Important
The tightening cycle also comes at a time when NBFCs are playing a significant role in extending formal credit to underserved segments, particularly micro and small enterprises.
Ravi Narayanan, MD & CEO, SMFG India Credit, said maintaining price stability remains important for smaller businesses because of its impact on their operating finances.
“For Bharat households and micro-enterprises, price stability protects real consumption and working capital,” Narayanan said.

The comment highlights a broader issue for NBFCs. Their borrowers are not equally equipped to absorb changes in financing costs. Micro-enterprises and smaller businesses with limited liquidity buffers can be more sensitive to changes in both borrowing costs and demand.

Narayanan also highlighted the role of the Account Aggregator framework in improving access to formal credit. Greater interconnectivity and access to financial data can help lenders assess cash flows more effectively, particularly where traditional documentation is limited.

For NBFCs, better underwriting can become increasingly important as the cost of capital rises. More accurate assessment of borrowers can help lenders maintain credit growth without compromising risk standards.
Liquidity To Remain Key Variable

The RBI’s management of system liquidity will therefore remain an important factor for NBFCs. The central bank has chosen liquidity-management tools rather than a reserve-ratio increase, while continuing to use bond sales and foreign-exchange swaps to manage liquidity conditions.

For NBFCs, changes in market liquidity can influence the availability and pricing of wholesale funds. Any sustained tightening in financial conditions could make refinancing more expensive, particularly for companies approaching large debt maturities.
At the same time, a resilient economy and strong underlying credit demand provide a counterweight.
The sector is therefore entering the next phase of monetary policy with two forces working in opposite directions: higher funding costs on one side and continued demand for credit on the other.

The RBI’s calibrated tightening stance means NBFCs may not face an abrupt change in business conditions, but the operating environment is becoming less forgiving. Funding resilience, borrower-level risk assessment and disciplined loan growth are likely to become more important as companies navigate the next phase of the rate cycle.
